title: Ryan T. Dobson
text:
The short version

I am a Ph.D. student in the Evolution and Society area of the Department of Psychology at the University of New Mexico. My research focuses on the evolutionary and developmental foundations of human social relationships and sexual behavior. Much of my work examines cross-sex friendships, relationship dynamics, and the developmental pathways that shape variation in sexual behavior.
I am broadly interested in integrating multiple methodological approaches—including genetically informed designs, longitudinal and intensive longitudinal data, and hormonal measures—to better understand how biological and environmental processes jointly influence human social and mating behavior.

title: Ryan T. Dobson
text:
What I work on

Three threads run through my work. Each one asks how biological and environmental processes jointly shape human social and mating behavior.



01

Cross-sex friendship and courtship
How mating motivations shape friendships between men and women, and how courtship behavior is signalled and perceived within them.

Mating psychology Relationships




02

Hormones and the ovulatory cycle
How women’s sexual psychology and emotional states shift across the cycle, and what estradiol and progesterone have to do with it.

Intensive longitudinal Endocrinology




03

Sexual development and behavior genetics
Using genetically informed designs to separate environmental effects from genetic confounding in how families shape sexual development.

Adoption designs Sibling comparison

title: Ryan T. Dobson
text:
Function families

The package currently exports around ninety functions. They fall into a few groups, most of which grew out of a specific analysis that I did not want to write twice.



Multilevel models
Within- and between-group decomposition, stepwise random-effects comparison, formula construction, and fixed-effect trimming.

mlm_groupmean() mlm_comparison() build_formulas()



Correlations
Publication-ready correlation matrices, including split tables that show two groups above and below the diagonal.

pub_cors_all() pub_cors_by() top_cor_diff()



Factor analysis and reliability
EFA summaries, factor loadings, scale reliability, and measurement invariance testing across groups.

efa_results() scale_reliabilities() test_measurement_invariance()



APA reporting
Model tables and reports formatted for APA style, with helpers to write them straight out to Word.

apa_lmer_model() apa_mlm_report() format_p()

title: Ryan T. Dobson
text:
Example functions

Each example below runs against fivelovelanguages, a cleaned dataset from my master’s thesis that ships with the package.



pub_cors_all()
pub_cors_all() quickly generates a publication-ready correlation table for a set of variables.

#grab specific variable names as a vector
ll_aos <- names(ll[, grepl("rec_aos", colnames(ll))])

#create a vector to display names nicely (optional)
nice_names <- c(
  "oral sex"        = "rec_aos_pt_1",
  "pleasing sexual" = "rec_aos_pt_2"
)

pub_cors_all(data       = ll, #dataset
             cor_vars   = ll_aos,  #vector of variabl names from the dataset to include in analysis
             rename_vec = nice_names, #named vector to map new variable names
             cor_use    = "pairwise", #defaults to "pairwise" deletion of cases
             rnd        = 2 #default rounds to 2
             )

pub_cors_by()
pub_cors_by() is an extension of pub_cors_all() that takes a dichotomous grouping variable and displays correlations for one group above the diagonal, and the other below.
It also prints the difference between the two groups’ correlations, which is a quick way to spot interaction effects. The group levels are read off the grouping variable, so you no longer have to name them yourself, and the grouping variable can be passed bare or as a string.

cors_by_sex <- pub_cors_by(data       = ll, #dataset
                           cor_vars   = ll_aos,  #vector of variable names from the dataset to include in analysis
                           group_var  = sex_bio, #levels are picked up automatically
                           rename_vec = nice_names, #named vector to map new variable names
                           cor_use    = "pairwise", #defaults to "pairwise" deletion of cases
                           rnd        = 2 #default rounds to 2
                           )

scale_reliabilities()
scale_reliabilities() computes reliability for several scales in one call, and tidy_scale_reliabilities() collapses the result into a single table you can drop straight into a manuscript.
Rather than just Cronbach’s alpha, it also reports omega total and a unidimensionality index, which is useful when you want to know whether treating a set of items as one score is defensible in the first place.

# pull the item sets for four of the love languages (reception format)
grab <- function(pattern) grep(pattern, names(ll), value = TRUE)

love_language_scales <- list(
  "Words of affirmation" = grab("^rec_woa_[0-9]+$"),
  "Quality time"         = grab("^rec_qt_[0-9]+$"),
  "Physical touch"       = grab("^rec_pt_[0-9]+$"),
  "Gifts"                = grab("^rec_g_[0-9]+$")
)

rel <- scale_reliabilities(ll, scales = love_language_scales)

tidy_scale_reliabilities(rel, rnd = 2)

                 scale   group    u alpha omega_tot
1 Words of affirmation overall 0.95  0.80      0.81
2         Quality time overall 0.94  0.85      0.85
3       Physical touch overall 0.83  0.72      0.74
4                Gifts overall 0.92  0.82      0.82


Passing a group argument returns the same table split by group, which makes it easy to check that a scale behaves similarly for everyone before you compare means across groups.

rel_by_sex <- scale_reliabilities(ll,
                                  scales = love_language_scales,
                                  group  = "sex_bio",
                                  groups = levels(ll$sex_bio))

tidy_scale_reliabilities(rel_by_sex, rnd = 2)

                 scale  group    u alpha omega_tot
1 Words of affirmation   Male 0.94  0.81      0.81
2 Words of affirmation Female 0.92  0.78      0.79
3         Quality time   Male 0.91  0.84      0.84
4         Quality time Female 0.94  0.82      0.82
5       Physical touch   Male 0.84  0.70      0.71
6       Physical touch Female 0.88  0.76      0.77
7                Gifts   Male 0.93  0.81      0.81

mlm_groupmean()
mlm_groupmean() is a function that helps to easily decompose variables into within- and between-group variance. This is a really handy function if you do any multilevel model analyses.

ll2 <- ll |> pivot_longer(cols      = c(rec_g_1, ex_g_1),
                              names_to  = "love_form",
                              values_to = "gift_1")
  mlm_groupmean(ll2,
              variables     = "gift_1",
              group         = "pid",
              within_affix  = "within_person_",
              between_affix = "between_person_",
              affix_type    = "prefix", #add a prefix. 'suffix' is the other option
              include_z     = TRUE #includes Z-scored versions of the variables
              ) |>
  select(matches("pid|gift_1|within_|between_")) |>
  arrange(pid) |>
  head()
